title: A talking therapy for young adults with depression that aims to reduce symptoms and prevent relapse
official: Preliminary effectiveness, feasibility and acceptability of a modular psychological treatment targeting depressive symptoms and relapse risk factors in young adults aged 18 to 25 years with depression: a single-arm case series in NHS Talking Therapies (DEpression Treatment for Young Adults)
summary:
Background and study aims 
Depression is common in young adults aged 18 to 25, and many people who recover go on to become depressed again (relapse). We have developed a cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)-based treatment for young adults that aims to reduce symptoms of depression and  also targets things known to make relapse more likely, such as rumination, loneliness and stress in relationships. It was developed with clinicians, academics and young adults with lived experience of depression. The treatment is split into modules, so each person and their therapist can choose the parts most helpful for them. This study aims to find out whether the treatment helps reduce depression symptoms, whether improvements last, whether it affects relapse risk factors, and whether it is acceptable to young adults and clinicians.

Who can participate? 
Young adults aged 18 to 25 who are seeking treatment for depression through North London NHS Talking Therapies.

What does the study involve?
Participants receive up to 20 sessions of the modular CBT-based treatment, usually weekly, in person or remotely. Before each session they complete the questionnaires routinely used in NHS Talking Therapies. They also complete study questionnaires before treatment, at the end of treatment, and 3 and 6 months later, and an interview about their symptoms at follow-up. At the end of treatment, participants and their clinicians are asked about their experience of the treatment and invited to an interview.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
Participants receive a treatment designed for their age group with an extra focus on preventing relapse. Their feedback may help shape future treatment for young adults. Talking about difficult topics in therapy or interviews may be distressing. The treatment is not expected to cause more distress than routine CBT, and clinicians are trained to provide support.

Where is the study run from? 
University College London (UK), with treatment delivered through North London NHS Foundation Trust Talking Therapies services.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
September 2026 to December 2027.

Who is funding the study? 
UCL Research Department of Clinical, Educational and Health Psychology (UK).

Who is the main contact?

interventions.name: Participants receive up to 20 sessions of a modular, CBT-based high-intensity modular psychological treatment for depression that aims to reduce symptoms of depression and target relapse risk factors. Practice elements included in the treatment modules were selected through a Delphi study with acade

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	18-25 years old
2.	Scoring ≥10 on the PHQ-9, i.e. being ‘in caseness’ for depression; having a degree of depressive symptoms considered to be indicative of probably meeting the diagnostic criteria for a Major Depressive Episode
3.	Seeking treatment for symptoms of depression  
4.	Ability to read and understand English sufficiently 
5.	Willing to attend treatment sessions and complete outcome measures
6.	Willing to provide written informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Seeking treatment for a mental health disorder aside from depression (e.g. an anxiety disorder)
2.	Currently receiving other psychological intervention(s) for depression 
3.	Change in psychotropic medication in the last 2 months or the plan to change during the study  
4.	Considered ‘high risk’ at assessment. This indicates the need for immediate or more specialised care e.g. acute suicidality or potentially life limiting self-harm
5.	Any intellectual disability limiting their ability to provide informed consent, understand the intervention or complete outcome measures

Participants presenting with manic, hypomanic or psychotic features will not be recruited. However, these individuals will have already been screened out during the NHS Talking Therapies assessment process as it is not the appropriate service for these patients.
